lines.text: Before the war, about twenty million barrels of oil passed through it every day. A fifth of all the oil the world uses.
On the twenty-eighth of February, the United States and Israel struck Iran.
Within hours, Iran's Revolutionary Guard was warning ships by radio. No passage.
By the eighth of March, Brent crude was above a hundred dollars a barrel, for the first time in four years. It peaked at one hundred and twenty-six.
A ceasefire in April. A memorandum signed in Islamabad in June.
Each time, the strait closed again.
This October, a ship has been struck there almost every day.
At American pumps, diesel broke its all-time record on the fourth of September. Last week it averaged six dollars twenty-eight a gallon. Two dollars sixty-six more than a year ago.
Diesel moves the trucks. So the price rides along with everything they carry.
In one week, Americans vote for all four hundred and thirty-five House seats, and thirty-five in the Senate.
In a Reuters Ipsos poll, forty-nine percent named the cost of living as the single most important factor in their vote.
And today, Israel votes. Its first election since the war began.
Twenty-one miles of water. And the bill arrives at the ballot box.
